passages.text:
[41~42] 다음 글을 읽고, 물음에 답하시오.

Famine, plague and war will probably continue to claim millions of victims in the coming decades. Yet they are no longer unavoidable tragedies beyond the control of a helpless humanity. Instead, they have become (a) manageable challenges. This does not (b) underestimate the suffering of millions of poverty-stricken humans; of the millions felled each year by diseases like malaria or pneumonia; or of the millions trapped in violent vicious circles in Syria or Afghanistan. The message is not that famine, plague and war have disappeared from life on Earth, and that we should stop worrying about them. Just the opposite. Throughout history people felt these were (c) unsolvable problems, so there was no point trying to put an end to them. People prayed to God for miracles, but they themselves did not seriously attempt to exterminate famine, plague and war. Those arguing that the world of 2016 is as hungry, sick and violent as it was in 1916 perpetuate this age-old defeatist view. They imply that all the efforts humans have made during the twentieth century have achieved nothing, and that medical research, economic reforms and peace initiatives have all been (d) effective. If so, what is the point of investing our time and resources in further medical research, novel economic reforms or new peace initiatives?

Acknowledging our past achievements sends a message of responsibility, (e) encouraging us to make even greater efforts in the future. Given our twentieth-century accomplishments, if people continue to suffer from famine, plague and war, we cannot blame it on nature or on God. It is within our power to make things better and to reduce the incidence of suffering even further.

* exterminate: 근절하다 ** perpetuate: 영구화하다

[43~45] 다음 글을 읽고, 물음에 답하시오.

(A)
Mr. Swift, a fourth grade teacher, once complained to me about a student, Steve, who seldom put effort into his work. He had adapted assignments to try to make them more interesting to him, and he had set firm limits, such as "You may not go to recess until you do your assignment." When nothing worked, Mr. Swift finally hit his limit. "You've got to stop being so lazy," (a) he warned Steve, "or you'll never get anywhere in this world."

(B)
Steve and Mr. Swift began to discuss what he could do differently so he could get more work done and how he might help with that. Steve's behavior didn't change overnight, but it did begin to improve slowly as he and his teacher experimented with those ideas. The shift toward constructive problem-solving happened only after Mr. Swift dropped (b) his use of the term "lazy" and focused on describing the behaviors that concerned him.

(C)
After listening to Mr. Swift, I asked what made him believe Steve was lazy. "Well," (c) he said, "he just sits through lessons fooling with things in his desk, and he only does about half of the work he's supposed to." "Try telling him that," I suggested, "without using terms like 'lazy.' And try to describe some things that (d) he does well, too." Together, Mr. Swift and I rehearsed some specific language that he might use.

(D)
After talking with me, Mr. Swift sat down with Steve in the classroom and described some of his more positive behaviors. "Steve, you're a friendly guy, and I've noticed that kids like to be around you." Then (e) he described the behaviors that concerned him. "I've also been noticing that you often play with things in your desk when it's time to listen to me, and you only finish about half of your assignments." "Oh," Steve said. After thinking a moment, he added, "I guess so, but it's hard to concentrate."

20. 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?

When I ask people for advice on how to age well, sometimes they smile and simply say, “Pick your parents wisely.” The emphasis we place on our genetics can often undermine the great deal of control we actually have over the aging process. One of the most undervalued or underappreciated aspects is the need to joyfully connect with others, whether with family, friends, or caretakers. We appreciate these social connections more as we get older, and for good reason — social support is often directly tied to healthy aging. Thus, a more empowering version of this saying is “Pick your friends wisely.” You might want to make good social connections, as being socially connected to people that are important to you may be one of the more underappreciated ways to stay healthy and enjoy old age.

21. 밑줄 친 Letting yourself go down a rabbit hole of assumptions가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?

Forcing myself to understand a situation before I react has been transformational. Make it a habit to pause in any circumstance that offends you, no matter how bad the offense may seem. So much energy and stress can be avoided if we try to understand why people are doing what they do; or, if necessary, we can avoid this wasted energy by deciding it is not going to affect our mood, no matter what. If you find out your spouse lied to you, your children lied to you, somebody at work is trying to undermine you, somebody at the gym is making fun of you, or someone went behind your back, stop and take a breath. After any upsetting event that happens in your life, taking a breath and refusing to react in the moment can lower your stress. Make the effort to understand where that person is coming from. Look through their eyes and then respond. <u>Letting yourself go down a rabbit hole of assumptions</u> is one of the largest energy-drainers there is. So make it a habit: decide not to do it.
choices: Taking relationships with other people around you for granted

Being highly sensitive to other people's needs and choices
Reacting without considering the real motive of people's actions

Innovators mobilize social networks to validate the usefulness of an innovation and its potential for success by exploiting past professional accomplishments and their own professional reputations. After all, the innovator has to demonstrate that he or she is the right person to carry the undertaking forward; a good plan is sometimes not enough to make a strong case for innovation when working with public sector authorities. That is why innovators work on giving evidence not only of a promising innovation but also of a capable innovator. Hermann Scheer, a German innovator, in promoting solar energy, knew that to impress stakeholders he would need more than just a great plan. To get support for his project, he had to boost his profile by reminding stakeholders of everything he had done before. He presented his case for solar energy to decision-makers not just as a good plan but as a good plan developed by a good man. He was not only a respected member of parliament but also a winner of the Right Livelihood Award for his efforts for sustainable energy production.

23. 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?

The rapid growth of the cinema during the interwar period focused attention on the potential influence of vast quantities of imported American cultural product. Films, in particular, were believed to be enormously powerful in their ability to shape public attitudes, values, and beliefs. The fear was that, along with American films, European audiences were subtly being Americanized. Anton Kaes argues that the cinema “was the most important factor in the European process of Americanization in the period of relative stabilization between 1924 and 1929.” This belief was widely enough held to deserve legal sanctions, not only to protect native film industries, but also to protect the native _mentalité_. The South German state government held at the time that “any foreign film was a threat to German culture.” James Hay reports that the “alien” values that films disseminated were seen at the time to have “corrupted the traditional foundation of Italian culture.” These reports reflect the emerging contemporary view of film as “a national resource.”

24. 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은? [3점]

Adam Smith’s theory of absolute advantage makes perfect sense when we consider the specialization of economic agents such as firms, but the firms implied in this model would be atomistic in nature. The theory of the firm consistent with Smith’s approach would not help us to understand the basis for specialization between nations in the real-world patterns of exports and imports of products. To explain more accurately the basis for specialization between economies, we have to turn to the theory of comparative advantage, put forward by economist David Ricardo. He suggested that a country can gain from exporting a product even when it does not enjoy an absolute advantage in production. Thus, it is possible that a successful exporting country might have a higher cost in terms of resources used in the production of a particular good than the importing country. This is counter-intuitive and seems like a recipe for disaster — but it is actually the basis for understanding why internationally trading nations should welcome the least productive economies into their community.

* atomistic: 별개로 독립된, 원자의
choices: Changes and Development of Comparative Advantage Theory
Comparative Advantage: Why Productivity Gaps Do Not Matter
How to Coordinate the Opposing Views on Absolute Advantage

26. Arturo Toscanini에 관한 다음 글의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?

Arturo Toscanini was born on March 25, 1867, in Parma, Italy. At the age of 9, Toscanini started to study the cello at the local music school. After his graduation, Toscanini joined a traveling opera company as a cellist. At the age of 19, when playing at the opera house in Rio de Janeiro, he was called upon to fill in for the conductor and performed Verdi's Aida from memory. Toscanini continued to serve as conductor for the remainder of the season, thus establishing his talent and reputation at the young age of 19. He came into prominence as a conductor in Italy and elsewhere. He conducted the New York Philharmonic-Symphony Orchestra from 1928 to 1936 and appeared with orchestras all over the world, except those of Italy during the Fascist regimes. On January 16, 1957, at the age of 89, Toscanini passed away at his home in New York City.

29. 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?

We can imagine the environment inside a young body as a highly ordered civilisation. The molecular streets are kept ① tidy and well maintained, every cell knows its job and its place, and any wrongdoers are taken out by the immune system. Only stem cells multiply, making new cells when they're needed, while the rest stand down, only ② springing into action in a state of emergency like an injury. Faulty and damaged cells die, while older cells that are no longer needed will quietly sit on the biological equivalent of the porch in a rocking chair, watching the world go by and minding ③ their own business. The stabilising and restrictive influence of young tissue must be ④ incredibly powerful, given that even outside influences that damage cells don't bring forward the onset of cancer too drastically. Unfortunately, nothing lasts forever. If young tissue is like a strictly regulated society, ⑤ which nothing is allowed out of place and dissent is not tolerated, then the inside of an older body starts to look a lot more like a free-and-easy neighbourhood where anything goes.

Liberals have long argued that greater interdependence between states — or ever greater and faster connections between states via trade, information, capital, and culture — changes international politics. Norman Angell famously argued, before World War I, that increased trade made war between the great powers too costly to rationally contemplate, so great power war could only be the result of ① irrational forces. Greater interdependence means more transactions and greater complexity, which means a greater need to ② coordinate activities and policies. Actors then gain a material interest in maintaining smooth flows and are more inclined to cooperate and support international institutions to manage the ③ increased complexity of intersocietal flows. Interdependence also affects the character of power. More interdependence means the bonds linking societies are ④ costlier to break, and military force is less and less useful. Because of the rise in complexity, power will tend to vary by issue area. Nye has argued that what he calls soft power (cultural influence and moral authority) is more ⑤ ineffective the higher the level of interdependence.
choices: irrational
coordinate
increased
costlier
ineffective

31. Academic research is a very _______________. We publish in journals available to all, meet up at conferences to exchange our most recent ideas, debate issues with colleagues around the world in email messages and spend hours discussing issues with the immediate members of our research groups. One consequence of this is that the origin of specific ideas may be hard to pin down. Occasionally, one gets into disputes where typically a research student or junior colleague accuses a senior colleague of stealing an idea. They may not be aware that their research supervisor could have deliberately planted some of their 'own' ideas in the first place, to help build their confidence. My experience is that research groups work best when people do not try to defend individual ownership of ideas but accept that they evolve through a group over time. As long as authorship of papers includes all relevant contributors, this rarely causes a problem.

32. The observation that people sometimes disregard obvious possibilities for improving their situation is empirically well-founded. An important example is provided by large investment decisions of firms. The general observation that individuals look at only a few possible outcomes also applies to managers considering investment in multinational corporations: The search for solutions is simple-minded, with the first acceptable alternative being adopted. Schmolders found that only half of the industrial corporations in Northrhine-Westphalia took more than one location into consideration, one quarter made a choice between two locations. A similar result appeared in an extensive survey of managerial perspectives on risk and risk-taking by March and Shapira: managers focus on very few aspects, and sequentially consider a relatively small number of alternatives, and sometimes only one single critical focal value commands all attention. Even managers acting under more competitive conditions consider only part of the whole objective possibility set, and may therefore stay at a point judged by outside observers _______________.

34. It is necessary to examine whether it's appropriate to suppose that a soul exists. St. Thomas Aquinas's argument supporting the existence of the soul begins by observing that some things are inert while other things are capable of movement, perception, thought, and desire. We call the former 'non-living' and the latter 'living'. If some bodies are living and others aren't, life can't be explained by the fact that a thing is a body. Aquinas contends that there must be some source that causes living things to be distinct from non-living things. This source can't be physical because if it were, then any material thing would be living, which is absurd. A body is alive not merely because it's a physical thing but because of a cause which isn't bodily or material. Without an immaterial soul, a body would simply be an empty shell. So it's the presence of a soul that _______________. [3점]

* inert: 비활성의
choices: draws a line between living beings sharing the identical cause
distinguishes animate beings from inanimate beings
separates spiritual essence from physical existence
transforms non-living matter into living beings gradually
explains how consciousness arises from physical complexity

35. 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?

Because humanization involves recognizing others as thinking, feeling beings, humanizing work requires organizations to provide work that recognizes employees' thoughts and feelings. ① This means giving people meaningful and challenging work and compensating them sufficiently, but it also involves something more. ② It involves ensuring employees do not feel disposable, mechanical, or commoditized in the face of automation — people have a deep need to be and feel irreplaceable. ③ To avoid these experiences organizations must provide work that engages employees' most distinctively human skills while providing sufficient leisure time to detach people's identities from their jobs. ④ Many individuals take part in activities that permit them to provide leadership in non-profit or religious organizations. ⑤ Leisure itself is a skill that robots can never master and, therefore, experiencing leisure whether through resting, listening to music, or simply letting one's mind drift enables people to feel "more than" automata.

* automaton: 자동 장치(pl. automata)

[36~37] 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것을 고르시오.

36.
The way that a smell receptor in the nose binds to a chemical is similar to the concept of a lock-and-key system. Each chemical has its own particular shape that fits into a specific protein receptor, just as each key has its own particular structure that fits into a specific lock.

(A) We interpret this as a particular smell. Scientists have recorded hundreds of individual aroma chemicals such as menthol and putrescine (responsible for the foul-smelling aroma that emanates from dead flesh). But any particular aroma we smell is usually the result of a mix of several chemicals.
(B) For example, while about half of the peppermint odor is due to menthol, the rest is a combination of more than thirty other chemicals. That's why we can describe the scent of an excellent spaghetti sauce, or of a deep red wine, or of a newborn baby in so many different ways.
(C) Only a unique chemical can bind to a unique receptor, and once this happens, it initiates a series of signals that ends in a nerve firing in the brain to let us know that the receptor has been stimulated.

* emanate: 나오다

37.
Regular rewards make recipients dependent on the supplier and subject to his power, since they arouse expectations that make their discontinuation a punishment.

(A) The air we breathe is not conceived by us to be a special reward, nor is the freedom to move about the streets as we please, but being suffocated or imprisoned is experienced as a punishment. Correspondingly, a man who has reason to expect to remain in his job does not think of his regular earnings as distinctive rewards, and the loss of his income is a punishment for him.
(B) The threat of being fired is a negative sanction that gives an employer power over his employees, enabling him to enforce their compliance with his directives. Regular rewards create expectations that redefine the baseline in terms of which positive sanctions are distinguished from negative ones.
(C) A person who has a job is rewarded for performing his duties by his earnings, and as his wages are positive sanctions it seems at first that no power is involved if power is understood as control through negative sanctions. However, being fired from a job cannot plausibly be considered to constitute merely the absence of rewards; it clearly is a punishing experience. [3점]

[38~39] 글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳을 고르시오.

38.
In the modern university, each individual student is free to pursue almost any interest, without having to be harnessed to what his intellectual ancestors thought was worth knowing.

There are many benefits to expanded educational opportunities. The traditional values and traditional bodies of knowledge transmitted from teachers to students in the past were constraining and often myopic. ( ① ) Until very recently, important ideas reflecting the values, insights, and challenges of people from different traditions and cultures had been systematically excluded from the curriculum. ( ② ) The tastes and interests of atypical students had been suppressed and frustrated. ( ③ ) But this freedom may come at a price. ( ④ ) Now, students are required to make choices about education that may affect them for the rest of their lives. ( ⑤ ) And they are forced to make these choices at a point in their intellectual development when they may lack the resources to make them intelligent.

* harnessed: 매여 있는 ** myopic: 근시안적인

39.
These desires are in eternal opposition, but are not necessarily antagonistic, any more than are the thumb and the little finger as they meet in some task.

William James points out that a man's interests and affections are his selves, and that they embrace one another like the petals of a rose. ( ① ) We may speak of unipetalar selves, who include only their own bodies in self-feeling; of bipetalar selves who include in it their families, and from there on we go to selves who include their work, their community, their nation, until we reach those very rare souls whose petals cover all living things. ( ② ) So men extend their self-feeling, if ambitious, to their work; if domestic, to home; if patriotic to the nation, etc. ( ③ ) Development lies in the extension of the self-feeling and in the increase of its intensity. ( ④ ) But the obstacle lies in the competitive feelings, in that dualism of man's nature that makes him yearn not only for friendship, but also for superiority. ( ⑤ ) Every function in our lives has its check and balance, and friendship, yearning and superiority urge one another. [3점]

* antagonistic: 적대적인 ** unipetalar: 홑잎의

40. 다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Psychologists have regarded recognition of emotion and attachment styles as universal. Thus, one might conclude that these topics should be easy to research: It would not matter where one conducted the research because people would not differ notably across different cultures. Unfortunately, current research on these topics contradicts the idea that cultural specifics are irrelevant. Consideration of attachment and of recognition of emotion reveals the difficulty that researchers face in trying to study constructs that may have some degree of universality. A further indication of the complexity of these issues is that constructs that may be regarded as similar may require very different cultural assessment. For example, with psychopathy, it appears that the structure of characteristics of psychopaths differs across cultures (Dutch and American) that one might assume are reasonably similar, being industrialized Western nations.
↓
Research of recognition of emotion and attachment styles is actually not (A) to conduct because research constructs in these issues may be considered (B) .

(A)          (B)
① simple …… culture-bound
② difficult …… context-specific
③ impossible …… outcome-oriented
④ obvious …… subject-centered
⑤ complex …… social-driven
choices: simple …… culture-bound
difficult …… context-specific
impossible …… outcome-oriented
obvious …… subject-centered
complex …… social-driven
